did_you_know.text: The verse notes Machir, Manasseh’s son, was a 'man of war' and so received Gilead and Bashan — territories east of the Jordan that strengthened the tribe’s position there.
Zelophehad had no sons but five daughters (names listed here: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah). Their case appears in Numbers and became important for inheritance rules when there are no sons.
The daughters appealed to both Eleazar the priest and to Joshua and the leaders — showing they brought their claim to religious as well as civic authorities.
Ten portions fell to Manasseh besides the lands of Gilead and Bashan — meaning Manasseh’s inheritance stretched on both sides of the Jordan.
Among the listed towns are junction sites like Megiddo and Beth‑shean — strategic locations in the Jezreel Valley that affected control of main routes.
They say they cannot drive out the inhabitants 'for iron chariots are there' — describing a military technological advantage, especially effective on plains like the Jezreel Valley.
